variants.title: Trace an alert to a decision
variants.context: An alert starts an investigation, it does not prove model failure. Evidence is layered: trust the record, measure what moved, join delayed outcomes, review impact on affected slices, then open a response gate. Skipping a layer turns a signal into an unsupported conclusion.
variants.prompt: A monitor pages an operator because one numeric feature moved this week. Put the investigation layers in order.

items.text: Join delayed labels using the model version, prediction time, entity, and decision policy.
Open the response gate: repair, contain, recalibrate, retrain, or keep observing with a stated validation boundary.
Compare reference and current inputs, predictions, attributions, and population slices.
Validate the record contract: types, units, ranges, nulls, category sets, freshness, and upstream releases.
Review impact: calibration, ranking, error rates, safety, and business outcomes on the affected slices.

variants.hint: Which layer decides whether the record can be trusted at all?
variants.explanation: Each layer rules out a different failure mode, so a response is chosen only after trust, movement, outcomes, and impact are established.

variants.title: Trace an alert to a decision
variants.context: An alert starts an investigation, it does not prove model failure. Evidence is layered: trust the record, measure what moved, join delayed outcomes, review impact on affected slices, then open a response gate. Skipping a layer turns a signal into an unsupported conclusion.
variants.prompt: A team is standing up drift monitoring for a model that just launched. Put the operating steps in order.

items.text: Observe a current window with enough samples to separate persistent movement from noise.
Diagnose before adapting: separate pipeline defects, population movement, prevalence change, and changed input-to-outcome relationships.
Freeze a reference: version the model, feature contract, population, time window, and evaluation slices.
Release a response: choose the smallest reversible intervention and validate it on the affected slices.
Join delayed outcomes as labels, user feedback, and business results become available.

variants.hint: Normal has to be defined before anything can be called abnormal.
variants.explanation: Without a versioned reference there is nothing to compare against, and without a diagnosis the response is a guess.

variants.title: Trace an alert to a decision
variants.context: An alert starts an investigation, it does not prove model failure. Evidence is layered: trust the record, measure what moved, join delayed outcomes, review impact on affected slices, then open a response gate. Skipping a layer turns a signal into an unsupported conclusion.
variants.prompt: Labels for this model arrive two weeks after the prediction. Put the runbook stages in order.

items.text: After release verify recovery, watch regressions, and record whether the alert was useful, noisy, or late.
When labels arrive measure task and business impact by slice and separate changed prevalence from changed conditional behavior.
At detection time preserve the model version, both windows, samples, detector configuration, and affected slices.
Before outcomes arrive validate contracts, inspect upstream changes, compare predictions, and contain severe exposure.
Before adaptation state the causal hypothesis, expected benefit, training window, acceptance tests, and rollback boundary.

variants.hint: The runbook is organized by what evidence exists yet, not by how loud the alert was.
variants.explanation: A runbook that survives delayed labels tells the responder what to do in each evidence state instead of waiting for labels to act.

variants.title: Release the fix safely
variants.context: Retraining or any fix is a model release, not an alert acknowledgement. Evidence runs from data validity to an offline comparison on the affected slice, regression coverage on protected slices, canary outcomes under real traffic, an agreed rollback boundary, and only then a new alert baseline.
variants.prompt: Labeled evidence confirms concept drift and a retrained candidate is ready. Put the release evidence in order.

items.text: Check regression coverage on protected historical, fairness, safety, and low-volume slices.
Publish rollback criteria naming the metric, threshold, and time window that reverses the wider release.
Keep a post-release watch and move alert baselines only after the new regime is understood.
Collect shadow or canary evidence with predictions and outcomes under realistic traffic.
Confirm data validity: contracts, lineage, and label joins pass for the candidate window.
Run the offline comparison: the candidate beats or safely matches the incumbent on the affected slice.

variants.hint: What has to be true about the data before any model comparison means anything?
variants.explanation: Recovery on the affected slice is not enough on its own, so regression coverage and live evidence come before the baseline is moved.

variants.title: Release the fix safely
variants.context: Retraining or any fix is a model release, not an alert acknowledgement. Evidence runs from data validity to an offline comparison on the affected slice, regression coverage on protected slices, canary outcomes under real traffic, an agreed rollback boundary, and only then a new alert baseline.
variants.prompt: The affected population is a small, high-risk slice that a global aggregate had hidden. Put the validation steps in order.

items.text: Expose the candidate to limited live traffic and watch product and safety metrics.
Compare candidate and incumbent offline on that slice alone, not on the global aggregate.
Hold the rollback path open until outcome evidence for the slice is mature.
Confirm protected historical and low-volume slices stay within bounds.
Verify the label join for that small population so its candidate window can be trusted.

variants.hint: The slice that triggered the incident is also the slice the evidence must cover.
variants.explanation: A global aggregate can hide a severe shift in a small high-risk population, so validation is run on that slice before traffic expands.

variants.title: Release the fix safely
variants.context: Retraining or any fix is a model release, not an alert acknowledgement. Evidence runs from data validity to an offline comparison on the affected slice, regression coverage on protected slices, canary outcomes under real traffic, an agreed rollback boundary, and only then a new alert baseline.
variants.prompt: Users report severe harm but labels are sparse and the cause is still uncertain. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Update the reference window only after the new operating regime is understood.
Contain exposure now by routing the affected population to a fallback or to human review.
Validate contracts and label joins for the window while evidence collects.
Compare the proposed change against the incumbent on the affected slice once labels arrive.
Expand traffic in stages with the rollback path still open.

variants.hint: When harm is confirmed but the cause is not, which action is both fast and reversible?
variants.explanation: Containment buys time for evidence without committing to a diagnosis, and updating the reference too early would normalize the incident.

variants.title: Name the shift
variants.context: Covariate shift moves P(X) while P(Y|X) is assumed stable. Prior probability shift moves P(Y) while P(X|Y) is assumed stable. Concept drift changes P(Y|X) itself. A data quality incident breaks the contract and only resembles a shift.
variants.prompt: A camera vendor change makes fleet images sharper. Labels still mean what they meant, and per-class appearance is consistent with the new optics. Which diagnosis fits?
options: Covariate shift, because the input distribution moved while label meaning held.
Concept drift, because the learned input-to-outcome relationship changed.
Prior probability shift, because outcome prevalence moved.
optionFeedback: Correct: P(X) moved through a new device mix while P(Y|X) is assumed stable.
Nothing here suggests the same input pattern now implies a different outcome.
The scenario reports no change in how often each outcome occurs.
variants.hint: Ask which probability actually moved: the inputs, the outcome rate, or the link between them.
variants.explanation: A new device mix changes image properties without changing what the labels mean, which is the definition of covariate shift.

variants.title: Name the shift
variants.context: Covariate shift moves P(X) while P(Y|X) is assumed stable. Prior probability shift moves P(Y) while P(X|Y) is assumed stable. Concept drift changes P(Y|X) itself. A data quality incident breaks the contract and only resembles a shift.
variants.prompt: An adversary learns the detection rule. Labeled outcomes show that transaction patterns which used to indicate fraud now belong to legitimate purchases. Which diagnosis fits?
options: Concept drift, because the same inputs now imply different outcomes.
Prior probability shift, because the positive rate changed.
Covariate shift, because the transaction mix changed.
optionFeedback: Correct: P(Y|X) itself moved, which is what an adversary or policy change produces.
The evidence is about meaning per pattern, not about how often fraud occurs.
The inputs may look similar; what changed is the outcome they predict.
variants.hint: Labeled outcomes are what separate a moved input from a moved relationship.
variants.explanation: When the same input pattern implies a different outcome, the learned relationship has changed and recalibration alone will not restore quality.

variants.title: Name the shift
variants.context: Covariate shift moves P(X) while P(Y|X) is assumed stable. Prior probability shift moves P(Y) while P(X|Y) is assumed stable. Concept drift changes P(Y|X) itself. A data quality incident breaks the contract and only resembles a shift.
variants.prompt: A seasonal campaign doubles the fraud positive rate. Within each class, labeled records look like they always did. Which diagnosis fits?
options: Concept drift, because the model now scores the population differently.
Data quality incident, because a contract must have broken upstream.
Prior probability shift, because outcome prevalence moved.
optionFeedback: Within-class patterns are unchanged, so the learned relationship is not what moved.
No schema, unit, category, or join change is reported here.
Correct: P(Y) moved while P(X|Y) is assumed stable, which is the seasonal prevalence case.
variants.hint: Check whether the per-class patterns moved or only how often each class appears.
variants.explanation: A prevalence change moves scores and thresholds without invalidating the ranking, so it is diagnosed separately from concept drift.

variants.title: Match cause to intervention
variants.context: The intervention follows the diagnosed cause. Repair a broken contract at its source, contain exposure when harm is severe but the cause is uncertain, recalibrate when scores still rank but prevalence or costs moved, and retrain when the learned relationship changed.
variants.prompt: An incident review lists four diagnosed causes. Match each cause to the intervention it calls for.

pairs.label: Broken contract
pairs.detail: Restore the schema, unit, join, or upstream feed and backfill the affected records.

pairs.label: Severe but uncertain
pairs.detail: Route to a fallback, narrow the eligible population, or require human review while labels arrive.

pairs.label: Scores still rank
pairs.detail: Adjust thresholds or calibration because prevalence or decision costs changed.

pairs.label: Relationship changed
pairs.detail: Train a candidate on representative labels and compare it against the incumbent.

variants.hint: Which causes can be fixed without touching the model at all?
variants.explanation: Retraining on a defect encodes the defect, so a broken contract is repaired at the source and only a changed relationship justifies a new model.

variants.title: Match cause to intervention
variants.context: The intervention follows the diagnosed cause. Repair a broken contract at its source, contain exposure when harm is severe but the cause is uncertain, recalibrate when scores still rank but prevalence or costs moved, and retrain when the learned relationship changed.
variants.prompt: Four alerts land in the same week. Match each observation to the response it justifies.

pairs.label: A category mapping silently changed upstream
pairs.detail: Repair the feed and replay predictions only where product semantics permit.

pairs.label: Harm is reported and labels are two weeks out
pairs.detail: Contain exposure and keep the rollback path open while evidence collects.

pairs.label: Prevalence doubled but ranking quality held
pairs.detail: Move thresholds and recalibrate the decision policy.

pairs.label: Labels show the same inputs now imply new outcomes
pairs.detail: Retrain a candidate and compare on current and protected historical slices.

variants.hint: Match on the evidence each observation actually supplies, not on severity.
variants.explanation: The response depends on cause, current harm, evidence maturity, and reversibility, so the same alert level can justify very different actions.

variants.title: Match cause to intervention
variants.context: The intervention follows the diagnosed cause. Repair a broken contract at its source, contain exposure when harm is severe but the cause is uncertain, recalibrate when scores still rank but prevalence or costs moved, and retrain when the learned relationship changed.
variants.prompt: A postmortem asks why each incident got a different treatment. Match each incident to its intervention.

pairs.label: A timestamp column starts arriving in a different timezone
pairs.detail: Repair the source and backfill before any model change is considered.

pairs.label: A small high-risk slice shows a large error increase with unknown cause
pairs.detail: Narrow the eligible population and require human review.

pairs.label: A policy update changed decision costs while score ordering held
pairs.detail: Re-tune thresholds instead of training a new model.

pairs.label: A market change makes historical patterns imply new outcomes
pairs.detail: Retrain on a representative window with protected historical slices held to bounds.

variants.hint: Ask what the model would learn if you retrained on this data today.
variants.explanation: Recalibration is the cheapest reversible fix when ordering still holds, and retraining is reserved for a genuinely changed relationship.

variants.title: Read the CDF gap
variants.context: The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the largest gap between two empirical cumulative distributions. At a given value it is the share of reference records at or below that value minus the share of current records at or below it.
variants.prompt: At 120 ms, 8 of the 10 reference latencies and 3 of the 10 current latencies are at or below that value, and this is the widest point in the sample. What is the KS distance?
variants.hint: The statistic compares shares of each sample, not raw record counts.
variants.explanation: The KS statistic is the maximum absolute difference between the two empirical cumulative distributions, here 0.8 minus 0.3.

mistakes.feedback: That is the difference in record counts; convert each count to a share of its own sample first.
That is the reference share alone, not the gap between the two shares.

variants.title: Read the CDF gap
variants.context: The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the largest gap between two empirical cumulative distributions. At a given value it is the share of reference records at or below that value minus the share of current records at or below it.
variants.prompt: A reference sample of 200 records has 150 at or below the cutoff. The current sample of 400 records has 200 at or below it, and this is the widest point. What is the KS distance?
variants.hint: Each sample is normalized by its own size before the two are compared.
variants.explanation: Unequal sample sizes are handled by taking 150 of 200 and 200 of 400 as proportions, giving 0.75 minus 0.5.

mistakes.feedback: That subtracts raw counts and ignores that the two samples are different sizes.
That is the reference share at the cutoff, not the gap between the two shares.

variants.title: Read the CDF gap
variants.context: The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the largest gap between two empirical cumulative distributions. At a given value it is the share of reference records at or below that value minus the share of current records at or below it.
variants.prompt: At the widest point, 40 percent of reference records and 85 percent of current records fall at or below the value. What is the KS distance, reported as a proportion?
variants.hint: The statistic is a proportion between 0 and 1, not a count of percentage points.
variants.explanation: The gap is 0.85 minus 0.40, and the statistic is always reported on the 0 to 1 scale of the cumulative distributions.

mistakes.feedback: That is the gap in percentage points; the statistic is reported as a proportion between 0 and 1.
That adds the two shares instead of subtracting one from the other.
